exam: A 28‑year‑old woman with 2 weeks of abdominal pain and fever has a right‑upper‑quadrant mass on exam. What is your next step and why? — Perform bedside abdominal ultrasound to look for a liver abscess; early imaging guides antibiotics and drainage.

In a patient with known cirrhosis presenting with tense ascites, what ultrasound finding would change management? — Detection of loculated fluid or septations suggests infected ascites (spontaneous bacterial peritonitis) requiring antibiotics and possible drainage.

How does ultrasound differentiate an ectopic pregnancy from a normal intra‑uterine pregnancy? — Intra‑uterine gestational sac with yolk sac confirms normal pregnancy; absence of intra‑uterine sac with adnexal mass or free fluid suggests ectopic.

A malaria‑positive child has hepatomegaly and fever. Ultrasound shows multiple hypoechoic lesions. What is the most likely diagnosis and treatment? — Likely hepatic malaria (schizontic lesions); treat with antimalarials and monitor lesion resolution on repeat scan.

Why is a large solitary hepatic lesion in a hepatitis B carrier concerning, and what ultrasound feature helps distinguish it from an abscess? — It raises suspicion for hepatocellular carcinoma; solid echogenicity with internal vascular flow on Doppler favors tumour over an abscess.

When is percutaneous drainage indicated for an abdominal collection seen on ultrasound? — When the collection is >5 cm, symptomatic, or not responding to antibiotics within 48 h; drainage reduces bacterial load and speeds recovery.

What red‑flag sign on obstetric ultrasound mandates immediate referral? — Empty uterine cavity with a gestational sac outside the uterus (adnexal mass) indicating ectopic pregnancy with risk of rupture.

If ultrasound is unavailable, how would you assess for ascites in a resource‑limited setting? — Perform shifting dullness and fluid wave tests; a positive result supports ascites and prompts therapeutic paracentesis if needed.
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Ultrasound is a bedside imaging tool that helps identify fluid collections, organ size, and focal lesions without radiation. In low‑resource hospitals it guides diagnosis when CT or MRI are unavailable. Understanding its indications, limitations, and common pitfalls is essential for safe patient care.

b: Non‑invasive, portable, no ionising radiation
Provides immediate bedside information
sections.p: Ultrasound uses high‑frequency sound waves to produce real‑time images of internal structures. It is operator‑dependent and best for evaluating fluid, solid organ size, and superficial masses.

Severity is graded by the extent of the abnormality seen (e.g., small vs large ascites, focal vs diffuse liver disease, single vs multiple abscesses). Staging follows disease‑specific criteria (e.g., WHO ascites grading).

b: Infective: pyogenic liver abscess, tuberculous peritonitis, schistosomal fibrosis
Chronic: hepatitis B/C‑related cirrhosis, alcoholic liver disease, sickle‑cell hepatic sequestration
Obstetric: ectopic pregnancy, intra‑uterine fetal demise, placenta previa
sections.p: In East African hospitals the most frequent reasons for an abdominal ultrasound are infections, chronic liver disease, and obstetric complications.

b: Right upper quadrant pain → consider liver abscess
Abdominal distension with shifting dullness → ascites
Amenorrhoea + pain → ectopic pregnancy
sections.p: Patients may present with abdominal pain, distension, fever, jaundice, or obstetric bleeding. Physical exam often reveals a palpable mass, shifting dullness, or a tender hepatomegaly.
Ultrasound is the first imaging test; other investigations are guided by its findings.

t.b: What organ or fluid abnormality is present? → Detects ascites, organ size, focal lesions; guides further work‑up
Is there an intra‑uterine pregnancy? → Confirms viability, location, gestational age; essential when ectopic is suspected
Do biochemical markers support hepatic disease? → Elevated bilirubin/ALT with cirrhotic pattern reinforces ultrasound findings

t.a: If ultrasound unavailable: bedside percussion & shifting dullness
t.b: Can fluid be detected clinically? → Provides provisional diagnosis of ascites when imaging is not possible

b: Rapidly enlarging abdominal mass → possible ruptured abscess
Severe hypotension with ascites → tense ascites causing respiratory compromise
Fetal heart rate abnormality on obstetric scan → intra‑uterine demise
sections.p: Complications arise when large fluid collections compress vital structures or when an infected collection ruptures.

b: Bacterial abscess → broad‑spectrum IV antibiotics (e.g., ceftriaxone) then percutaneous drainage if >5 cm
Ascites from cirrhosis → sodium restriction, diuretics (spironolactone + furosemide), therapeutic paracentesis if tense
Ectopic pregnancy → methotrexate for stable, unruptured cases; surgery if haemodynamically unstable
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then address the ultrasound‑detected abnormality with supportive measures.

b: Re‑scan after 48‑72 h of antibiotics to confirm abscess shrinkage
Serial scans for ascites after diuretic titration
Screen for hepatitis B/C, HIV, and schistosomiasis in chronic liver disease
sections.p: Repeat ultrasound to assess response; address modifiable risk factors.

b: Ascites vs large ovarian cyst → both cause abdominal distension; cyst shows a well‑defined anechoic structure, ascites is free fluid
Liver abscess vs hepatic tumour → abscess has irregular walls, central debris; tumour is solid, may have vascular flow on Doppler
sections.p: Conditions that mimic ultrasound findings on clinical exam.

b: Obesity limits acoustic windows → may miss small lesions
Gas‑filled bowel can obscure liver lesions → consider alternative imaging if suspicion remains
Early pregnancy (<5 weeks) may not be visualised → repeat scan after 6 weeks if ectopic still suspected
sections.p: Certain scenarios produce false‑negative or misleading images.
